title: Rook pawn: the draw
summary: The rook pawn's two key squares, the race of the kings and the defences that save half a point.
part.keySquares.title: The two key squares
part.keySquares.summary: With a rook pawn only g7 and g8 matter, and the black king on f8 is already enough to draw.
part.lock.title: The king locked in the corner
part.lock.summary: The white king in front of its pawn does not win: Black locks it in on h8.
part.race.title: The race to the corner
part.race.summary: One king runs to g7, the other to f8. Whoever gets there first decides the game.
part.kingFirst.title: King first, and the h7 exception
part.kingFirst.summary: The pawn does not help in the race, with one exception worth knowing.
part.summary.title: Defending from afar, and the summary
part.summary.summary: Barcza's route against Fischer and three rules to take to your games.
step.t_keys: In the king and pawn lesson you saw that the king in the corner draws. Here the black king is not there yet. White to move: which move wins, and why do almost all the others draw?
step.t_keys.hint1: Forget the pawn for a moment. What does the black king want to do on its next move?
step.t_keys.hint2: Look at the two squares next to the corner, g7 and g8. Whoever gets close to them first decides.
step.keys: A rook pawn has only two key squares, and they never change: g7 and g8. Pawn on h2 or on h6, it makes no difference. If my king steps on one of them, the black king never reaches the corner again, and the pawn walks up on its own. That is why Kg7: the black king is left outside.
step.keysLock: Now the same position with Black to move. Kf7! and my king has neither g7 nor g8. It may stand in front of the pawn, but it is stuck there. For the defender the rule is the mirror image: reaching f8, or the square in front of the pawn, is already a draw.
step.d_keys: See how simple it is when the white king arrives first. The black king chases the pawn and never catches it.
step.d_keys.m1: Kg7. The king enters the key square and shuts the corner.
step.d_keys.m2: The black king tries to come back through the centre.
step.d_keys.m3: Now the pawn moves. The king on g7 looks after its path.
step.d_keys.m4: The black king comes closer, but from the outside.
step.d_keys.m5: h5. The pawn keeps going; the black king is still far away.
step.d_keys.m6: It threatens to go after the pawn via g5.
step.d_keys.m7: h6, and this is the only move: the pawn runs to the square my king protects.
step.d_keys.m8: Too late for the black king.
step.d_keys.m9: h7, and next it becomes a queen. The king on g7 did all the work.
step.keysMove: White to move and win. The black king wants to come back via e7 and f8. Don't let it, then bring the pawn up.
step.keysMove.hint: Put your king on a square that takes e7 and e8 from the black king, right next to the road to g7.
step.keysMove.done: That's it. With the king on f7 (or f6) Black never reaches f8, and the pawn walks up in peace.
step.t_lock: Now you defend. The white king is already in front of the pawn, in the corner. It looks lost. Where must your king stand so that nothing happens?
step.t_lock.hint1: The white king has to leave the corner for the pawn to pass. Which way would it go out?
step.t_lock.hint2: The exits are g7 and g8. One square on the f-file watches both.
step.lock: This is the prettiest defence against a rook pawn. The white king stands in front of its own pawn, and that is its problem: for the pawn to move, the king must leave through g7 or g8. With the black king on f7 or f8, both doors are shut. The white king is locked in, and the pawn is only good for stalemate.
step.d_lock: I'll defend with Black. Notice that my king only steps between f7 and f8.
step.d_lock.m1: Kf7. I shut g7 and g8 at once.
step.d_lock.m2: White pushes the pawn, because the king has nothing useful to do: it can only shuffle between h8 and h7.
step.d_lock.m3: Kf8, no hurry. g7 and g8 stay shut.
step.d_lock.m4: The pawn reaches h7, and now the white king has no square at all.
step.d_lock.m5: Kf7, and White has no move: stalemate. Draw.
step.lockMove: Black to move and draw. The white king is in the corner. Get there in time to lock it in.
step.lockMove.hint: Head for the f-file, close to g7 and g8, and stay around there.
step.lockMove.done: Perfect. The white king is locked in the corner, and the pawn alone can do nothing.
step.t_panno: Panno against Najdorf, Buenos Aires, 1968. The rooks have just come off and White is to move. The black king is far away, but so is the white one. Who wins the race?
step.t_panno.hint1: Count how many moves the white king needs to reach g7, and how many the black king needs to reach f8.
step.t_panno.hint2: Both need four moves. So whose turn it is decides.
step.panno: This is a race, and the pawn takes no part in it. The white king heads for g7, the black king for f8. White climbs the g-file, Black walks along the seventh rank, and both are four moves away. With White to move, the white king gets there first. Najdorf, one of the greats of his time, had just played Kb7 and was already lost.
step.d_panno: The game, and what would have followed. Panno wastes no time on the pawn.
step.d_panno.m1: Kg4. The race begins; the pawn waits on h2.
step.d_panno.m2: Najdorf runs too, along the seventh rank.
step.d_panno.m3: Kg5. Still one step ahead, and here Najdorf resigned. The rest is analysis.
step.d_panno.m4: Had he played on, the black king would keep running.
step.d_panno.m5: Kg6. One more move and the white king is on g7.
step.d_panno.m6: The black king reaches e7, one step from f8.
step.d_panno.m7: Kg7, the only winning move. The door on f8 is no use any more.
step.d_panno.m8: The black king turns back to chase the pawn.
step.d_panno.m9: Only now does the pawn move.
step.d_panno.m10: The black king threatens to reach g4.
step.d_panno.m11: h5, the only move again. The pawn runs away, and the king on g7 guards the rest of the road.
step.najdorf: And if it were Black's move? Same count, but now the black king starts first. Kc7, Kd7, Ke7 and Kf8: it reaches the corner area before the white king gets to g7, and it is a draw. A single tempo separates the win from the draw. Now you defend.
step.pannoDraw: Black to move and draw. Run to f8 by the shortest road.
step.pannoDraw.hint: Walk along the seventh rank to e7, then step to f8.
step.pannoDraw.done: You made it. King on f8, and the white king never steps on g7. That is what Najdorf lacked: the move.
step.t_shoulder: White to move and win, but only with one move. Pushing the pawn looks natural. Is it?
step.t_shoulder.hint1: Where does the black king want to go? It has to pass through the f-file.
step.t_shoulder.hint2: Think of a king move that stands in the black king's way, not one that runs straight to g7.
step.shoulder: Here the reflex of pushing the pawn spoils everything: h4? and the black king comes via f5 and f6 to f7. The right move is Kg6. My king does not go straight to g7: it steps into the way and takes f5 and f6 from the black king. With its body it pushes the other king away.
step.d_shoulder: See how the black king has to take the long way round.
step.d_shoulder.m1: Kg6. f5, f6 and f7 are mine now.
step.d_shoulder.m2: The black king tries through the centre.
step.d_shoulder.m3: Now the pawn can move: the black king can no longer reach it.
step.d_shoulder.m4: It looks for e7 and f8.
step.d_shoulder.m5: h5, and the pawn keeps going.
step.d_shoulder.m6: The black king reaches e7, but too late.
step.d_shoulder.m7: Kg7, the key square. From here the pawn promotes.
step.exception: I said f8 draws. There is an exception, and it is a famous one. King on g6, pawn on h6, black king on f8 and White to move. The pawn goes to h7, and the black king cannot reach the square in front of it: g7 belongs to my king, g8 to the pawn. It is the one case where the pawn does the job by itself.
step.exceptionMove: White to move and win. This is the exception: the pawn does the work.
step.exceptionMove.hint: The black king needs g7 or g8. Who takes those squares?
step.exceptionMove.done: That's it. With Black to move this would be a draw: Kg8, and the black king settles in front of the pawn.
step.barcza: Now the other side of the board, and the other side of the table. Barcza against Fischer, Zurich, 1959. The queens have just come off, and Fischer is left with the rook pawn against Barcza's bare king. The white king looks far from the corner, but the square it needs is c1, the twin of f8 for a pawn going down. Along the diagonal, it gets there. The draw was agreed right here.
step.barczaMove: White to move and draw. Take the king to c1, then into the corner.
step.barczaMove.hint: Go down the diagonal towards c1. Don't let the black king reach b2 before you.
step.barczaMove.done: Done. The white king is on b1, next to the corner, and Fischer has no way to drive it out.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: a rook pawn has two key squares, g7 and g8; the attacker races for them. Second: the defender races for f8, or for the square in front of the pawn; from there he locks the white king in the corner or settles in it himself. Third: it is a race of kings; count the moves, remember the pawn does not help, and check whose turn it is. Now play Black and draw.
step.finish: Black to move and draw. The white king is closer to the pawn. Find the road to f8.
ex.e01: White to move and win. The pawn is on the a-file. Which is the key square?
ex.e01.hint: For an a-pawn, the key squares are next to the corner, on the b-file.
ex.e01.solution: Kb7, or Kb8: the king steps on a key square and the black king never reaches c7 or c8 in time to lock it in. The other moves let the black king reach c7, and then it is a draw.
ex.e02: Black to move and draw. The white king is locked in the corner. Keep it there.
ex.e02.hint: The white king can only get out through b7 or b8. Keep an eye on those squares.
ex.e02.solution: Kc8 (or Kc6). The black king keeps watching the exit, and the white king stays in the corner. Moving the king to the d-file lets the white king out.
ex.e03: White to move and win. The black king is on the square that usually draws. Why not today?
ex.e03.hint: It is the exception. Who controls b7 and b8?
ex.e03.solution: a7! The white king takes b7 and the pawn takes b8. The black king cannot stop the promotion. With Black to move it would be a draw: Kb8.
ex.e06: Black to move and draw. The white king is right next to g7. Only one move holds.
ex.e06.hint: The white king's two exits are g7 and g8. A single square shuts both.
ex.e06.solution: Kf7! shuts g7 and g8 at once. Any other move lets the white king into g7 or g8, and then the pawn promotes.
ex.e07: Black to move and draw. The white king is near the corner. Don't let it reach g7.
ex.e07.hint: Go to the f-file and, when the pawn advances, watch g7 and g8.
ex.e07.solution: Kf6 (or Kf5) and, after h5, only Kf7: the black king shuts g7 and g8. After Kh7, Kf8 (or Kf6), and the white king is locked in.
ex.e09: White to move and win. Pushing the pawn looks natural. Which move wins?
ex.e09.hint: The black king wants c7 and c8. Put your king in its way before touching the pawn.
ex.e09.solution: Kb6! The white king takes c5, c6 and c7 from the black king. Then the pawn moves up (or the king goes to b7) and the black king is too late. a4? lets the black king come via c5 and c6 to c7, and it is a draw.
ex.e10: Black to move and draw. The black king is on the other side of the board. Is there still time?
ex.e10.hint: The shortest road to f8 is a diagonal. Count the moves.
ex.e10.solution: Kc3!, Kd4 and Ke5: the black king crosses the board along the diagonal and reaches f7 or f8 in time. Any other first move loses a tempo, and that tempo decides.
ex.e11: White to move and win. Only one move keeps the win, and it is not a pawn move.
ex.e11.hint: The black king wants f8. From which square does your king take e7 away and still reach g7?
ex.e11.solution: Kf6! takes e7 and prepares Kg7. After Ke8, Kg7 and the pawn promotes. Any other move lets the black king reach f8 in time.
key.keys: The rook pawn's key squares: g7 and g8. White to move wins with Kg7; Black to move draws with Kf7. Position from Audax6's study on Lichess.
key.lock: The white king locked in front of its own pawn: with the black king on f7 or f8, it is a draw.
key.pannoNajdorf: Panno–Najdorf, Buenos Aires 1968. White to move: Kg4 and the king reaches g7. Black to move: Kc7 and the king reaches f8.
key.shoulder: King first: only Kg6 wins; h4? lets the black king reach f7. Position from Audax6's study on Lichess.
key.exception: The exception: with White to move, h7 wins even with the black king on f8.
key.barczaFischer: Barcza–Fischer, Zurich 1959. Kd2 and Kc1 draw; the draw was agreed in this position.
history: The rook pawn is the worst pawn to have and the best one to face. Endgame manuals treat it on its own: Wikipedia, quoting Jeremy Silman, sums it up in the two key squares next to the corner. Two great players were saved or lost by it. In Zurich, 1959, the young Fischer won Barcza's last pawn and was left with an extra rook pawn; Barcza's king was two moves from c1, and the draw was agreed on the spot. In Buenos Aires, 1968, Najdorf reached the same ending with Black, but with White to move: Panno ran his king to g7 and Najdorf resigned two moves later. The difference was a single tempo.
practice: Now against the machine. You are the black king in the Panno–Najdorf position, but with the move. Run to f8 and hold the draw.
